draft.title: Breach, causation and loss
card: To win a civil claim, the plaintiff must show three things: a breach, causation and a loss. If one is missing, the claim fails.
Breach
the defendant broke a legal duty or obligation, such as a duty of care or a term of a contract.
Causation
the breach caused the harm. The harm must have happened because of the breach, not for some other reason.
Loss
the plaintiff suffered real harm, such as injury, damage to property or lost income. A breach with no loss gives nothing to compensate.
draft.remember: A civil claim needs all three: a breach, that caused the harm, and a loss.

a.q: Which situation is a loss, as needed for a civil claim?
opts: A cyclist cannot work for a month because of a broken arm
A driver ignores a stop sign but no one is nearby
A shop promises delivery by Friday and delivers on Monday
A neighbour plays loud music but you are away all week
a.why: A month of lost work is real harm, in the form of injury and lost income. Ignoring a stop sign may be a breach, but with no harm to anyone there is no loss.
a.clue: Look for actual harm, not just a rule being broken.

b.q: Leo hires Priya to paint his fence. She finishes a week late, which breaches the contract. The fence is later damaged by a storm. Leo sues for the storm damage. Why is his claim likely to fail?
opts: The breach did not cause the storm damage
There was no breach of the contract
Leo did not suffer any loss
Storm damage cannot be claimed in court
b.why: Priya's lateness was a breach, and the fence was damaged, so a loss exists. But the storm caused the damage, not the late work, so causation is missing. A claim needs all three elements.
b.clue: Ask what actually caused the damage.

a.best: A cyclist cannot work for a month because of a broken arm

b.best: The breach did not cause the storm damage

problems.detail: 'If one is missing, the claim fails' overstates the rule. It holds for negligence, but a breach of contract can still succeed for nominal damages without proven loss. Some wrongs, such as defamation and trespass, are actionable without proof of loss. Softer wording would be accurate, such as 'usually needs' or 'the claim will usually fail or gain little'.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear right answer each. The card's statement that a claim always fails if any element is missing is too absolute, because a breach of contract can still win nominal damages, so it should be softened.
